## Before anything else - do you have Git?

1.  Open a terminal and run `git --version`.
2.  A version number = you're ready. An error = install Git now, and keep up with the slides while it runs:

- Download the installer for **any operating system** at [**git-scm.com/downloads**](https://git-scm.com/downloads), and accept the defaults
- macOS shortcut: `xcode-select --install` in the terminal does it too
- Inside WSL/Ubuntu: `sudo apt-get install git`

## Configure Git - introduce yourself

Git stamps every commit with an author, so tell it who you are (once per computer):

``` bash
# Set your name and email
# use the SAME email as your GitHub account

git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "your.email@example.com"

# Make every new repository start on a branch named 'main'
# (older Git versions default to 'master' - set this once and forget it)

git config --global init.defaultBranch main

# Check your settings

git config --list
```

# Using Git and GitHub

## Git and GitHub

### What is Git?

- **Git** is a distributed version control system
- Tracks changes in your code over time
- Allows collaboration with others
- Maintains complete history of all changes

### What is GitHub?

- **GitHub** is a web-based hosting service for Git repositories
- Provides cloud storage for your code
- Enables collaboration features
- Hosts documentation and websites (GitHub Pages)
- Free for public repositories

## GitHub for Scientific Collaboration

### Perfect for Research Projects:

- **Reproducibility**: the complete history of how every figure was made - "code available at github.com/yourlab/..." is what journals and funders increasingly require
- **Collaboration**: labmates and collaborators work on the same analysis - no more emailing `script_final_v3_REALLY.R` around
- **Lab continuity**: when a student graduates, the analysis stays - with the history of why each choice was made
- **Documentation**: README files, wikis, and GitHub Pages
- **Issues**: track bugs, ideas, and to-dos right next to the code
- **Releases + DOIs**: tag the exact version used in a manuscript; linking Zenodo turns a release into a citable DOI
- **Reuse**: most published pipelines live on GitHub - clone them, read them, build on them

## Git Workflow Concept

![Git workflow: working directory, staging area, local and remote repositories](../images/Lec09_img001.svg){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

- **Track Changes**: Every modification is recorded
- **Collaboration**: Multiple people can work simultaneously
- **Backup**: Your code is safe in multiple places
- **Experimentation**: Try new things without breaking working code

## Git Branching and Collaboration

![Branching and merging](../images/Lec09_img002.svg){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

- Today we stay on one branch, `main`
- The commands for branching and merging are in the *For later* slides at the end and in [Ch. 19](../book/chapters/19-git-github.html)

## Authenticating to GitHub

Pushing needs more than your password - GitHub stopped accepting passwords from the command line in 2021, and the first `git push` is where everyone gets stuck. We'll all use the **GitHub CLI** (`gh`), the easiest route:

``` bash
# 1. Install the CLI

brew install gh                  # macOS
winget install --id GitHub.cli   # Windows
sudo apt-get install gh          # Ubuntu / WSL

# 2. Log in - one time only

gh auth login

# gh now asks four questions in the terminal; pick these answers:
#   "Where do you use GitHub?"            answer: GitHub.com
#   "Preferred protocol?"                 answer: HTTPS
#   "Authenticate Git with credentials?"  answer: Yes
#   "How would you like to authenticate?" answer: Login with a web browser
#
# It then prints a one-time code: copy it, press Enter, and paste the
# code into the browser window that opens. That's the whole login.

# 3. Confirm it worked

gh auth status                   # "Logged in to github.com as USERNAME"
```

::: callout-tip
Done once, done forever on this machine. The alternatives - SSH keys (which also log you in to Talapas in Week 10) and credential managers - are in [Ch. 19](../book/chapters/19-git-github.html#sec-git-auth).
:::

# Creating repositories

## Walkthrough: a new repository, from your laptop to GitHub

We'll do this live, together - a brand-new repository on your computer, then the same repository on GitHub, then the two connected:

``` bash
# 1. Make a project and put it under version control

mkdir ~/projects/git_practice && cd ~/projects/git_practice
git init                      # creates the hidden .git/ folder
git status                    # read what it says - always

# 2. Create a few files worth tracking

echo "# My first repository" > README.md
echo 'print("hello, git")' > analysis.py
echo "lab notes, day 1" > notes.txt

# 3. Stage - three ways to say what goes into the commit

git add README.md             # one file, by name
git add *.py                  # wildcard: every .py file
git add .                     # everything new or changed from here down

# 4. Commit the staged snapshot

git commit -m "First commit: README, analysis script, notes"
git status                    # "working tree clean" - everything is recorded
```

::: callout-tip
Fall behind? Keep watching - every step of today's class is in [Ex 8](../Exercise_Folder/Exercises_Week08.qmd) to redo tonight at your own pace.
:::

## Best Practices: commits

### Messages - the history is for readers (including future-you)

- First line short (\~50 characters) and imperative: "Add violin plot", not "Added some stuff"
- Say *why*, not just what - the diff already shows the what
- Bad: `stuff`, `final`, `final2`, `fixed it` · Good: `Normalize counts before PCA`

### Habits

- Commit **early and often** - one logical change per commit, so the history reads like a lab notebook and any single step can be undone
- `git status` and `git diff` before every commit - know exactly what you are recording
- **Pull before you start, push when you stop** - the habit that keeps two machines (or two people) out of trouble

## Viewing Commit History

``` bash
# View commit history

git log

# Prettier one-line format

git log --oneline

# With graph

git log --graph --oneline --all

# Show changes in commits

git log -p

# Show last n commits

git log -3
```

## What changed? `git diff` and commit hashes

``` bash
# What have I edited but not yet staged?

git diff

# What is staged, about to be committed?

git diff --staged

# Every commit has a unique ID - a hash. See the short form:

git log --oneline        # e.g.  7d4e8c2  Add violin plot

# Compare any two commits by their hashes

git diff 7d4e8c2 3f9a1b5
```

- A **hash** is the commit's name - quote it in lab notebooks ("results from `7d4e8c2`") and use it anywhere a command wants a commit
- **HEAD** is simply the commit you are standing on right now; `HEAD~1` is one commit back

## Walkthrough: connect it to GitHub

First, make the repository's empty home on GitHub - we'll click through this together:

- On [github.com](https://github.com): **+** (top right) → **New repository**
- Name it `git_practice`
- **Leave it completely EMPTY** - no README, no license, no .gitignore (those would start a history that conflicts with yours)
- Click **Create repository** - the next page shows a *"...or push an existing repository from the command line"* box
- **Copy YOUR repository's URL from that box** (it contains *your* username - don't type mine from the screen)

``` bash
# Connect and push - the same lines GitHub just showed you

git remote add origin https://github.com/USERNAME/git_practice.git
git branch -M main            # make sure your branch is named 'main'
git push -u origin main       # -u: remember this pairing for future pushes
```

::: callout-note
**Why `branch -M main`?** Older Git creates the first branch as `master` (harmless if yours is already `main`) - and GitHub takes the **first branch you push** as the repository's default, so push `main` first and the two sides agree.
:::

## The round trip: `pull`

Your repository now lives in **two places** - so finish the loop:

``` bash
# 1. On github.com: open README.md, click the pencil icon,
#    add a line, and commit the change THERE

# 2. Bring that commit down to your laptop

git pull

# 3. Proof - both commits, one history

git log --oneline
```

- `push` and `pull` are the same verb in opposite directions - this is also how you'll move between laptop and Talapas in Week 10
- **Daily rhythm** from here on: `git pull` → edit → `git add .` → `git commit -m "..."` → `git push`

::: callout-tip
Lost or confused? `git status` always tells you the next command. And worst case: your work is on GitHub - delete the folder and `git clone` it back.
:::

## Why `.gitignore`? Not everything belongs in history

- Git never forgets: every version of every tracked file stays in the repository **forever** - perfect for code, terrible for bulk files
- Much of a project folder doesn't need tracking: raw data (it never changes - record *where it lives* instead), outputs you can regenerate, editor and system droppings (`.DS_Store`, `.Rhistory`), package caches
- GitHub enforces this economy: a file over **100 MB is rejected** outright (warnings start at 50 MB), and a repository should stay **under 1 GB** - 5 GB at the outside
- The fix is a `.gitignore` file: a list of patterns Git pretends not to see
- Write it **first**, before `git add .` - ignoring a file that is already committed does not remove it from the history

## .gitignore File

### Exclude files from version control:

``` bash
# Create .gitignore file
touch .gitignore
```

### Common patterns to exclude:

``` bash
# Data files
*.fastq
*.fasta
*.bam
*.vcf
data/raw/*

# R files
.Rhistory
.RData
.Rproj.user

# Python files
__pycache__/
*.pyc
.venv/
.ipynb_checkpoints/

# Output files
results/temp/*
*.log

# Quarto working folder
.quarto/

# System files
.DS_Store
```

## Best Practices: what belongs in a repository

```         
project/
├── README.md          # Project description - the front page on GitHub
├── .gitignore         # What Git should never track
├── data/              # Raw data (usually .gitignore'd - README says where it lives)
├── analysis/          # Analysis scripts (.R, .py, .sh, .qmd)
├── results/           # Output files (commit small tables/figures; regenerable ones can be ignored)
└── docs/              # Documentation, or the rendered website for Pages
```

- **Yes**: code, text, notebooks, config, `environment.yml` (next week) - small, human-readable, hard to recreate
- **No**: large raw data (put *where it lives* in the README), regenerable bulk output, `.quarto/`
- **NEVER**: passwords, API keys, tokens - even in a private repository; treat every commit as permanent and public

# GitHub Pages

## GitHub Pages: host your research website for free

![From Quarto source to a live website](../images/Lec09_img003.svg){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

- Any repository can serve a website: **Settings → Pages → Deploy from a branch → `main`, `/docs`** - live at `https://username.github.io/repo_name`
- Quarto fits perfectly: `output-dir: docs` in `_quarto.yml` means `quarto render` fills `docs/` and a push publishes it (`quarto publish gh-pages` is the one-command alternative)
- Which is exactly what we do next, live

## Finale: last week's website goes live

In L07 you built `example_website` - a real four-page Quarto site (home, research, publications, CV) with your details in it. A website is just a folder of HTML files; GitHub Pages will serve that folder to the world. Step one is getting the folder rendered and under version control:

``` bash
cd ~/projects/my_website        # your website project from last week

# 1. Render the site one final time
#    _quarto.yml says output-dir: docs, so the finished HTML
#    lands in docs/ - open docs/index.html to see what will go live

quarto render
touch docs/.nojekyll            # tells GitHub Pages: serve the files as-is

# 2. Exactly the walkthrough from earlier - plus the .gitignore,
#    so Quarto's working folder stays out of the repository

git init
echo ".quarto/" > .gitignore
git add .
git commit -m "First commit: my academic website"
git branch -M main
```

*(No website from last week? Grab `example_website.zip` from the [Examples page](../Examples.html#week-7), unzip it, put your name in `_quarto.yml` - two minutes, then rejoin.)*

## Finale: flip the switch

``` bash
# 3. On github.com: New repository -> my_website -> EMPTY again
#    (no README, no license - your history already exists locally)

git remote add origin https://github.com/USERNAME/my_website.git
git push -u origin main
```

4.  On GitHub: **Settings → Pages → Deploy from a branch → `main`, `/docs` → Save** - you are telling GitHub "serve the `docs/` folder of `main` as a website"
5.  Watch the repository's **Actions** tab: a "pages build and deployment" job runs for about a minute and turns green
6.  Open **`https://USERNAME.github.io/my_website`** - on your phone too; it is the public internet now
7.  Updating the site from here on is just the daily rhythm: edit a `.qmd` → `quarto render` → `git add .` → `git commit` → `git push` - live about a minute later

::: callout-tip
That URL is real, permanent, and free - put it in your email signature. It is also the exact mechanism your term project report will use.
:::

## Start now: publish your personal website

The finale you just watched is *your* homework - the personal academic site you started building last week becomes real this week:

1.  Finish personalizing it: your name, your research, your CV pages (started in L07; no copy? `example_website.zip` on the [Examples page](../Examples.html#week-7))
2.  `quarto render` → `touch docs/.nojekyll` → `git init` → commit - exactly today's finale, on your own machine
3.  Push it to a new repository and flip on **Pages** - your site, at your URL, in your email signature by Friday
4.  From then on, every improvement is just render → commit → push

::: callout-tip
The same publish loop ends **HW2** (goes out today, due Monday, November 30: analysis → Quarto report → pushed to GitHub) and the **term project** (due Friday, December 11, with a README like the [example](../Examples.html#week-8)). One mechanism, three deliverables.
:::

## Where is my site's URL - and can I change it?

**Finding it:**

- **Settings → Pages** shows *"Your site is live at https://USERNAME.github.io/REPO_NAME"* with a **Visit site** button once the deployment finishes
- The pattern is always `USERNAME.github.io/REPO_NAME` - the repository's name is the last part of the URL, so name repositories accordingly
- The **Actions** tab shows every "pages build and deployment" - green check = your newest push is what's live

**Nicer names:**

- Name a repository exactly **`USERNAME.github.io`** and its site lives at the bare root, `https://USERNAME.github.io` - the classic home for your personal site
- A fully custom domain (`www.yourname.org`; \$10-20/year at any registrar): **Settings → Pages → Custom domain**, add the DNS record your registrar asks for (a `CNAME` pointing at `USERNAME.github.io`), and tick **Enforce HTTPS**
- With Quarto, keep a file named `CNAME` (containing just the domain) in the published folder - list it under `resources:` in `_quarto.yml` so every render re-creates it

## Summary - and where we are in the arc

- **Git** records every step; **GitHub** backs it up, shares it, and (with **Pages**) publishes it
- The arc so far: shell pipelines → R/Python scripts → data frames and figures → Quarto documents → a published, reproducible project
- Still to come: **environments that travel** (next Monday, L09) and **Talapas at scale** (L10) - the last two pieces of the loop
- Every tool here is free, open, and the daily standard in computational science

# For later - on your own

## Branching and Merging

`git switch` (and `git restore`, two slides on) are the modern commands that split the overloaded `git checkout` in two - older tutorials say `checkout`, and both forms work:

``` bash
# Create and switch to new branch

git switch -c feature-branch

# Switch branches

git switch main

# Merge branch

git merge feature-branch
```

## Common Git Workflow with Branches

### Daily Development Cycle

``` bash
# 1. Start your day - update your local copy

git pull origin main

# 2. Create a feature branch

git switch -c new-feature

# 3. Make changes and commit regularly

git add .
git commit -m "Add new analysis function"

# 4. Push your branch

git push origin new-feature

# 5. Create pull request on GitHub (via website)
```

## Undoing: `git restore` and resetting HEAD

``` bash
# Discard your edits to a file (back to the last commit) - GONE for good

git restore analysis.R

# Un-stage a file, keeping your edits

git restore --staged analysis.R

# Undo the last commit, three strengths:

git reset --soft HEAD~1    # undo commit, keep changes staged
git reset HEAD~1           # undo commit, keep changes unstaged
git reset --hard HEAD~1    # undo commit, DISCARD the changes
```

::: callout-warning
`restore` (without `--staged`) and `reset --hard` delete real work with no confirmation. Run `git status` and `git diff` first, so you know exactly what you are throwing away. [App. H](../book/chapters/appendix-H-git.html) has the full undo table.
:::

## Cloning an Existing Repository

The other way a repository reaches your laptop - someone else's (or yours, on a new machine):

``` bash
git clone https://github.com/username/repository.git
cd repository    # a full copy: files, history, remote already connected
```

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
